physical.title: cloth
physical.summary: Textile (perhaps a baby-tie or a sash), aso oke, composed of four strips of imported European cotton in two shades of brown, which have been hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvedges. The warp is formed of alternating narrow stripes of either shade of brown. A complicated pattern is created in the weft using three decorative weaving techniques: alternating the ground weft between the two shades of brown; adding bundles of threads of supplementary weft; and creating circular or oval holes by tying warp threads together and carrying the lines of twisted warp threads from one hole to the next (‘aso eleya’: the last two techniques are specific to the Yoruba). The textile has been hemmed by hand.

physical.title: textile; cloth
physical.summary: Cloth (Yoruba aso oke), composed of 16 hand-woven narrow strips, hand-woven from imported cotton, and hand-sewn together along the selvedges. The ground weave is entirely white in the warp and most of the weft, though the weft also has lines of pink; there is a supplementary weft in purple but in no other colour. Each of the two outer strips has an individual design, one with pairs of pink lines in the weft, the other with six pattern blocks arranged regularly along its length with hour-glass designs in purple bordered by bands of pink. The 14 strips in the centre of the cloth all have the same design, which is more or less accurately aligned across the cloth. There are three bands of decoration using (a) diamond shapes formed by discontinuous ground weft in pink, (b) hour-glass shapes formed by supplementary weft in purple, and (c) stripes with open-work created by binding the weft. The ends have been hemmed by hand.

The panel has been divided into squares, six along the warp and three across the weft, and each of these has a geometric pattern (some of them repeated) formed by stitched groups of lines. The squares stop short of the ends of the cloth, which are now plain indigo. The cloth has been hemmed, and is now discoloured yellow, apparently by exposure to sunlight.

physical.title: adire
physical.summary:
Adire cloth: woman's: composed of two even lengths of machine plain woven European cotton machine sewn together. The textile is decorated using the starch resist method. The producer has applied the starch by hand before dyeing the textile indigo. The textile is called IBADAN DUN or 'Ibadan is sweet'. The textile is decorated in 21 different patterns:
Row 1, square 2 (from left): Umbrella and cassava leaves
Row 2, square 1: the pillars of Mapo Hall
Row 2, square 2: guinea fowl
Row 4, square 2: ostrich
Other patterns which can be identified (and all its patterns are in fact representational) are:
Row 2, square 3: Koran board and forks
Row 4, square 3: Ifa divination board with two hedgehogs

The hems are machine sewn and signed by the maker.

physical.title: adire
physical.summary: Adire cloth: woman's: made of textile plain woven European cotton. Composed of 10 narrow strips of imported cotton stitched together and hemmed on a sewing machine. Each individual strip has been folded and rolled lengthwise then rapped with cotton thread then dyed using indigo. This creates the ELELO or ' the owner of tinting (coiling)' pattern. This name refers to the method of manufacture. This method creates alternating warp stripes.

physical.title: adire
physical.summary: Adire: a single panel of imported European white calico cotton cloth, dyed in Nigeria using a stencil and starch resist to create a repeat pattern of spiral circles in 8 by 17 rows across the cloth. W.B.Fagg recorded that the pattern was known as 'Olokoto' (='snail shell').
